claims: Unilateral and bilateral landings are mechanically distinct, so takeoff foot count and landing foot count are identity fields rather than synonyms.
An exact quarter-turn card must also declare rotation magnitude and direction, displacement, terminal hold, side accounting, and reset.
Quarter-turn jump and hop tasks belong to plyometric jump-and-landing work, but unilateral and bilateral modes remain separate controlled identities.
The canonical family records aerial reorientation and terminal stabilization without using athlete proficiency labels.
A 90-degree whole-body reorientation and landing uses coordinated lower-limb deceleration plus pelvis and trunk control; the two legs may not share landing load equally.
Cards declare foot, ankle, knee, hip, pelvis, trunk, and visual-orientation demands without claiming isolated muscle activation or injury prediction.
Mid-flight whole-body rotation changes landing mechanics compared with a nonrotational landing and requires control of angular momentum and reorientation before stabilization.
The authored bilateral task uses two-foot takeoff and two-foot landing; the authored unilateral task uses one declared leg for takeoff and same-leg landing.
Unilateral landing changes knee motion and muscle demand compared with bilateral landing and therefore receives a higher physical-difficulty and stabilization score.

Complexity also accounts for exactly 90 degrees of aerial orientation, foot-count contract, landing alignment, hold, side completion, and reset; overall difficulty is the maximum of complexity and physical difficulty.
Every takeoff and landing is counted in the session impact budget, with unilateral contacts tracked by side.
Contact volume, prior jumping and running exposure, surface, amplitude, landing strategy, symptoms, and recovery state must be considered before selection or progression.
The task requires a level high-traction resilient surface, clear takeoff and landing zone, visible orientation target, safe footwear, and enough space for an uncontrolled step without collision.
Pain, instability, lower-limb restrictions, dizziness, inability to follow the stop command, or an exhausted impact budget block selection.
Dose is stored as fully reset attempts and total landing contacts rather than a fatigue circuit or vague work interval.
The card starts with small sets, long enough rest for repeatable orientation and landing quality, and lower volume on the unilateral task.
Instruction declares start orientation, takeoff and landing foot contract, exact quarter turn, target, quiet aligned landing, hold duration, and reset before the next attempt.
Feedback is concise and externally observable; it does not promise injury prevention or prescribe a universal joint angle.
Landing direction changes lower-limb biomechanics, so each direction and side is screened and coached rather than assumed equivalent.
Stop for symptoms, under- or over-rotation, wrong-foot contact, audible or stiff impact, knee-foot or trunk-control loss, balance step before the hold, fatigue drift, unsafe surface, or traffic.
Quarter-turn stick landings are low-volume output or landing-control exposures performed while fresh, not sustained conditioning.
Workout generation must validate phase, impact budget, side balance, rest, surface, space, exact foot contract, and substitutions after every change.
Athlete support explains the exact foot contract, what a controlled stick looks like, expected effort, unexpected symptoms, self-checks, and how to request a lower-impact alternative.
Pain or instability is a stop signal, not a difficulty target.
Coaches observe turn magnitude, takeoff and landing feet, asymmetrical loading, trunk orientation, knee-foot alignment, landing noise, hold, symptoms, side completion, and reset.
Group delivery requires one athlete per marked zone, a shared start and stop signal, clear turn direction, and a maintained sightline.
Unilateral and bilateral options are not interchangeable accessibility labels; an easier option changes the exact exercise and requires a reviewed substitution.
Accessible delivery can reduce jump height and attempts, increase rest, use larger visual targets, and provide text, still-image, audio, or live instruction while preserving the chosen identity.
Landing support, direction, displacement, external load, approach, obstacle or drop, rotation magnitude, terminal action, and reactive cue are evaluated separately.
Clockwise versus counterclockwise direction and starting side are modifiers only after takeoff, landing, displacement, rotation, and finish are fixed.
YouTube oEmbed health and embedding metadata establish current candidate availability only.

A human must watch the complete video and verify exact foot contract, 90-degree rotation, displacement, terminal hold, cueing, safety, captions, accessibility, and demonstration quality before approval.

assessmentSummary.identity: From a stationary two-foot stance, take off from both feet together, turn exactly 90 degrees in the air in the declared direction with minimal horizontal displacement, land on both feet together facing the target orientation, hold under control, and reset before the next attempt.
currentCardFindings: This is a new research-authored exact definition; it is not a consolidation of either ambiguous legacy source.
Two-foot takeoff, two-foot landing, exactly 90 degrees of whole-body rotation, minimal displacement, terminal hold, and full reset are identity-bearing.
Clockwise or counterclockwise direction, starting orientation, jump height, attempt count, hold duration, and rest are delivery modifiers after identity is fixed.
Five oEmbed-healthy title candidates are retained without exact-match or quality approval.
